newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan officials forecast calm after dollar drop.
newsitem.headline: Japan officials forecast calm after dollar drop.

text.p: Japanese authorities, who just last week were talking down the dollar, shifted gears on Monday in an apparent effort to keep its slide from going too far.

Speaking after the dollar fell below 118 yen to its lowest level in nearly four months, Japan's "Mr Yen", a top finance official who earned that monicker for his influence in markets, told reporters the dollar was likely to "settle down soon".

The comments by Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, were quickly echoed by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka and top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama.

"I think the message of the G7 (Group of Seven) nations' agreement on foreign exchange rates is gradually getting through to the market," Mitsuzuka, who along with Sakakibara was in Fukuoka, southern Japan for a meeting of the Asian Development Bank, told reporters. "As a result of the message getting through, it will settle down soon."

Financial leaders of the G7 -- Japan, the United States, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- said in Washington last month that they would monitor exchange rates and cooperate as appropriate. They said currency values should reflect fundamentals and excess volatility was not desirable.
Market players at the time shrugged off what they saw as a weak G7 statement, pushing the dollar to a peak of 127.47 yen on May 1.

Last week, however, Sakakibara jolted jittery markets by saying the yen could strengthen as far as 103 yen to the dollar, and the U.S. currency's fall picked up momentum as speculation spread that it may have turned the corner after a two-year rebound.
Panic selling in early Asian trade on Monday sent the dollar as low as 117.50 yen, but it then rebounded to lick its wounds and was stable at just under 119 yen in mid-afternoon.

Japanese authorities have appeared keen to see the yen strengthen because of U.S. worries that a weak Japanese currency would cause Tokyo's trade surplus to balloon again and spark a new bout of trade friction with Washington.

But the weak yen has been a clear plus for Japan's economy because of the boost it gives to exports by making them more price competitive. The yen's fall had also cheered the Tokyo stock market by making blue-chip exporters an attractive buy.
Some currency analysts said Japanese authorities were now soft-pedalling their earlier push for a stronger yen, in hopes the rise would not go too far.
"They're backing off a little bit. The weak yen is actually good for Japan's economy," one currency strategist said.

Some analysts warned that the dollar could still spring back against the yen, but added that it was unlikely to challenge fresh highs. "The (dollar's) upward trend was probably dented very severely by the most recent moves," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
What the future holds depends not only on Japan's trade surplus, but also on interest rate trends in Japan and the United States, analysts said.
Japan has kept its interest rates at rock-bottom levels since September 1995, when it slashed its official discount rate to 0.5 percent to keep its economic recovery on track.

Speculation has emerged that the Bank of Japan might tighten its hyper-easy credit stance due to growing confidence in the recovery. But doubts remain whether the central bank will do so quickly, given economic uncertainties and worries over the burden of problem loans at many Japanese banks.
Comments by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan in New York on Friday, meanwhile, left room for doubt over whether the Fed would raise rates when it next meets on May 20.
